newsitem.title: UK: Uday Hussein says he mentally, physically normal.
newsitem.headline: Uday Hussein says he mentally, physically normal.

text.p: Uday Hussein, eldest son of the Iraqi president, said in an interview shown on Friday that he was mentally and physically normal after gunmen tried to kill him last December.
Uday said he had seen the faces of his would-be assassins and indicated he believed they were Iranians who attacked him in his car as he drove along a Baghdad street.
"They did not look like Arabs, they looked different," Uday told CNN television.
"Arabs have beards like mine. Iranians have larger beards. In general we can differentiate clearly between Arabs and Iranians," said Uday, sporting a neatly trimmed beard.
Speaking in English through an interpreter, he added: "Time has proved that Iran is involved in such incidents."
It was Uday's first interview since the shooting and thought to have been granted in order to show he was beginning to recuperate and to dispel speculation about his condition.
One British Sunday newspaper even reported that he had died after the attack.
Sitting in a wheelchair in a Baghdad hospital, Uday moved his hands in order to show they were not paralysed, and said: "If you are asking about my mental and physical abilities, they are normal."
He said he hoped that after an operation "there is a good possibility that I will be able to engage in sports again".
Uday said he had been hit in various parts of the body, including both his legs. He had been severely wounded in the left leg, which had suffered a double fracture.
Iraqi and French surgeons would shortly operate on his left leg.
He had already undergone surgery to remove a bullet and pieces of shrapnel from his body.

Asked if he considered himself to be President Saddam Hussein's heir apparent, Uday told interviewer Ben Wedeman that if he had not been a foreigner he would probably have been punished for asking such a question.
Uday said he did not have any security guards with him when he was shot, and the attack did not indicate any weakness in the Iraqi security apparatus.
He denied that a state of emergency had been imposed, as had been reported.
"This sort of incident could take place anywhere. It doesn't mean our security services are weak," Uday said.
He said the assassination bid had been carefully planned and it would take time for an Iraqi investigation to reach any conclusions.
He said the results of the investigation would be made public.
The attack appeared to have left Uday in a philosophical frame of mind.
"Bullets can tear flesh, but flesh can be stitched. A bone is broken, but it can be mended.
"The most important thing is the spirit. The more trouble the spirit is exposed to, the stronger its principles become," he said.
